strengths: Novel and timely threat model: the paper is among the first to formulate an input-aware backdoor attack specifically targeting visual grounding in VLMs, addressing a genuine open-vocabulary challenge (attack target varies per image) rather than assuming a fixed trigger/label pair as in classic backdoor attacks.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: experiments span three VLMs with different grounding capabilities (LlaVA, Ferret, InternVL), four datasets (RefCOCO/+/g, COCO-2017), an ablation study, poison-rate sweep, transferability study, defense evaluation, inference-time overhead measurement, and qualitative real-world photos/screenshots.
The unified attack-data generation procedure (constructing poisoned triplets from existing grounding annotations) is practical and could be reused by follow-up work.

Evaluation against several representative defense families (spectral, Gram-matrix-based, perturbation-based) shows the attack is not trivially caught by existing generic defenses, which is a useful empirical finding for the community.
The paper is transparent about attack success rates being moderate rather than near-100%, and offers a plausible explanation tied to the open-vocabulary/generative nature of the task.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Sections 5, Appendix A) is largely a sequence of informal invocations of universal approximation and PL-condition results, with strong unstated assumptions (e.g., a 'unique-activation rule' is simply assumed rather than derived, and the gate function p(I) is asserted to exist and approximate g(I) without any construction tied to the actual U-Net/VLM architecture). It reads as decorative rigor rather than adding real insight into why or when the attack works, and does not connect quantitatively to the empirical results.

Absolute ASR@0.5 values (roughly 30-70%) are moderate, and while the paper offers a rationale, this tempers the claimed severity of the security threat compared to typical backdoor attack literature where ASR near 100% is standard.

The comparison to prior attacks (BadEncoder, TrojVLM) is performed only after simplifying them to an artificial closed-vocabulary, 100-target setting, which is not directly comparable to IAG's open-vocabulary formulation; this could bias the comparison in IAG's favor and makes it hard to assess relative merit fairly.

Description of the trigger injection mechanism is inconsistent/underspecified: the main text defines It = Gθ(Ib, zO) + Ib as simple addition, but Figure 2 labels the same operation 'Mix-up', and no ablation isolates the effect of the injection method itself (only 'w/o mixup' appears, without clarifying what the mixup actually differs from the additive formula in text).

Stealthiness claims rely solely on a reconstruction loss and a few qualitative case-study images (Figure 3), some of which show visible artifacts; no quantitative perceptual-quality metrics (e.g., SSIM/LPIPS/PSNR) or human perceptibility study are reported to substantiate the 'imperceptible trigger' claim.

The threat model assumes the attacker controls the full fine-tuning process and poisons the training set, which is a strong assumption; the paper does not discuss how realistic this is in comparison to more common data-poisoning-only threat models, nor whether the attack survives further benign fine-tuning/re-alignment after backdoor injection.

The 'w/o LLM loss' ablation trivially collapses to 0% ASR/BA in all settings, which is an expected/uninformative result (removing the primary training signal breaks the model entirely) rather than a meaningful diagnostic of the proposed design choices.

Real-world validation (Appendix G) is limited to a handful of qualitative examples with a single victim model/dataset configuration and no quantitative success rate, limiting the strength of the claimed real-world applicability.
Related work discussion of closely related semantic-trigger backdoor attacks (e.g., BadSem) is brief and mostly used to assert novelty rather than to analyze similarities/differences in depth.

strengths: Identifies a novel and realistic threat model: input-aware, multi-target backdoor attacks on VLM-based visual grounding, moving beyond prior static-trigger/fixed-target assumptions, with a plausible real-world motivation (GUI agents, embodied AI).

The proposed text-conditioned UNet trigger generator is a reasonable technical design choice, well-motivated against simpler baselines (linear mappers, shallow autoencoders), and the joint training objective balancing LM loss and perceptual reconstruction loss is clearly formulated.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three VLM architectures (LLaVA, InternVL, Ferret) and five datasets/benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI), with consistent improvements over four baselines in most settings.

Strong supplementary analysis: ablations on loss components and hyperparameters, imperceptibility metrics (PSNR/LPIPS/L1), robustness against multiple detection- and sanitization-based defenses, poison-rate sensitivity, transferability across datasets and to VQA tasks, attention visualization for interpretability, and real-world photo/screenshot case studies substantially strengthen the paper's claims.
Includes a theoretical margin-based analysis (Proposition 1) attempting to justify why input-aware triggers outperform fixed triggers, adding some formal grounding beyond purely empirical claims.

Comparison against reproduced static-target VLM backdoor baselines (BadVLMDriver, TrojVLM, VLOOD) adapted to the multi-target setting demonstrates the necessity of the input-aware design, not just superiority over classification-domain baselines.
weaknesses: ASR values, while highest among baselines, remain moderate (25-68%), and the paper does not fully characterize failure modes or provide statistical significance/variance across runs, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1) rests on several strong, loosely justified assumptions (local linearization, target-aligned feature shift with high probability) that are not empirically validated or connected quantitatively to the observed ASR values; it reads more as a qualitative justification than a rigorous guarantee.

Baselines are exclusively adapted from image classification backdoor literature (One-to-N, Imperio, Marksman) and hastily-reproduced VLM-specific static attacks; there is no comparison to any purpose-built input-aware VLM backdoor method, partly because none exist, but this leaves open whether the improvements stem from the specific UNet design versus simply from having any input-aware, semantically informed generator.

The attack requires full fine-tuning/LoRA access and joint training of the trigger generator with the VLM, plus poisoned data with attacker-controlled triples; the threat model, while stated, could be discussed more critically regarding how realistic/easy it is for attackers to control this joint training pipeline in practice versus simpler data-poisoning-only settings.

Real-world case studies and visualizations are qualitative/anecdotal (a handful of images) rather than systematic quantitative evaluation, limiting the strength of claims about real-world applicability.

Some presentation issues: dense notation in the theoretical section, and results tables are large and could benefit from clearer summarization of key takeaways; the paper relies heavily on appendix content for core claims (defenses, transferability, real-world evaluation) that arguably belong more centrally to the evaluation.

strengths: Identifies and formalizes a novel, realistic threat model: multi-target, input-aware backdoor attacks specifically tailored to VLM-based visual grounding, which differs meaningfully from prior static-trigger/fixed-target backdoor attacks on VLMs.

The proposed text-conditioned U-Net trigger generator with cross-attention conditioning and skip connections is a reasonable architectural choice, and the joint training objective (LM loss + perceptual reconstruction loss) is well-motivated to balance effectiveness and stealth.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three VLM architectures (LLaVA, InternVL, Ferret) and five datasets/benchmarks (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg, Flickr30k Entities, ShowUI), with consistent gains over reasonably chosen adapted baselines (Imperio, Marksman, One-to-N).

Good coverage of auxiliary analyses: imperceptibility metrics (PSNR/LPIPS), ablations on architecture choices and hyperparameters, evaluation against multiple detection-based and adaptive defenses, poison-rate sensitivity, inference-time overhead, transferability across datasets/tasks, benign-task retention, and qualitative real-world case studies.

The paper includes an attention-map visualization and a lightweight theoretical margin analysis that, while informal, provide some intuition for why input-aware/text-conditioned triggers should outperform static ones.
Clear real-world motivating scenarios (GUI agents, embodied AI) that make the threat concrete and relevant to practical VLM deployment.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Proposition 1) relies on strong, unverified assumptions (local linearization of the visual-to-language pathway, a clean low-dimensional trigger subspace, high-probability gradient alignment) that are not empirically validated; the 'proof' reads as a plausibility sketch rather than a rigorous guarantee, and it does not meaningfully predict or explain the specific numeric results in the experiments.

Because there are no directly comparable prior methods for this exact threat setting, all baselines are re-purposed from classification-oriented backdoor attacks (Imperio, Marksman, One-to-N); while reasonable, this makes claims of 'best ASR' harder to contextualize against attacks natively designed for generative/grounding outputs.

Reported ASR values are moderate (roughly 25–70%), well below near-100% rates typical of classical backdoor attacks; although the paper offers a plausible explanation (large space of unseen targets), this somewhat limits the practical severity of the demonstrated threat and is not deeply analyzed (e.g., no breakdown by target frequency/rarity or object category difficulty).

Imperceptibility claims rest primarily on PSNR/LPIPS proxy metrics and a handful of qualitative examples; no human perceptual study is conducted to substantiate that the trigger is genuinely unnoticeable to end users across varied content.

Real-world evaluation (Appendix Q) is purely qualitative (a handful of case studies) without quantitative success-rate measurements in these real conditions, limiting the strength of the 'real-world threat' claims.

The method assumes attacker access to a frozen benign embedding layer of the same architecture for text conditioning at inference time; this dependency and its practical implications for attack deployment/generalization across differing tokenizers or embedding spaces are not deeply discussed.
Only mid-sized (7–8B) open-source VLMs are tested; no evaluation on larger or proprietary/closed models, so generalization of the vulnerability to state-of-the-art large VLMs remains unconfirmed.

As a dual-use/attack paper, the ethical safeguards described (Section S) are largely generic statements about responsible disclosure rather than concrete mitigations, and no defense mechanism is proposed, leaving the core security concern raised by the paper largely unaddressed beyond an evaluation of existing defenses' failures.
